tiers.name: Randomised
tiers.identifying_assumption: Random allocation gives exchangeability: treated and untreated groups differ only by chance, in measured and unmeasured characteristics alike.

tiers.name: Local as-if random
tiers.identifying_assumption: An assignment rule or instrument isolates exogenous variation — but only where its own conditions hold, and those conditions are themselves testable claims.

tiers.name: Comparison-group panel
tiers.identifying_assumption: Parallel trends — the treated and comparison groups would have moved together absent the intervention — or weighted comparison units that tracked the treated unit before it.

tiers.name: Selection on observables
tiers.identifying_assumption: No unmeasured confounding given the measured covariates. Untestable in principle; the argument rests on substantive knowledge of the assignment process.

evidence_scales.maryland_note: Level 3 where pre-period outcomes are used as controls and comparability is demonstrated rather than asserted.

tiers.name: Single time series
tiers.identifying_assumption: The pre-intervention trend would have continued unchanged. No comparison group exists to falsify this, so it stands or falls on the plausibility of the counterfactual trend.

roles.when: Every counterfactual tier is Blocked, or there are too few units for any counterfactual comparison to be informative.
A counterfactual tier is available. Theory-based work then addresses mechanism, implementation and context — questions an effect estimate cannot answer.

views.argument: Identification rests on a continuity assumption across a date, which is a time-series claim: nothing else changed at the cutoff. That is the same class of assumption as a comparison-group panel, not local randomisation.

views.qualifier: where a sharp administrative cutoff in time is externally imposed
views.argument: Treated as a discontinuity design proper, on the grounds that the running variable is a genuine assignment rule.
The control series supplies a comparison group, placing it with the panel designs rather than with as-if-random assignment.
Sometimes grouped with quasi-experimental designs of higher internal validity where the control series is strongly comparable.

contested_placements.subject: Matching and weighting with prior-outcome controls

views.argument: Still selection on observables — conditioning on prior outcomes narrows the scope for unmeasured confounding but does not remove it.
Where pre-period outcomes are used and comparability is demonstrated, the Maryland scale allows level 3, which maps to Tier 3.

designs.name: Individual RCT
designs.estimand: ATE among those randomised

designs.name: Cluster RCT
designs.estimand: ATE where groups are the unit of allocation
designs.notes: Feasibility is driven by the number of clusters and the ICC, not by total participants

designs.name: Stepped-wedge RCT
designs.estimand: ATE averaged over exposure time
designs.notes: Requires a phased rollout that already exists and whose order can be randomised

designs.name: Crossover RCT
designs.estimand: Within-person ATE
designs.notes: Requires a reversible outcome and an adequate washout period

designs.name: Waitlist RCT
designs.estimand: Short-run ATE before the control group crosses over
designs.notes: Everyone is eventually treated; the effect is identified only before crossover

designs.name: Encouragement design
designs.estimand: ITT of the encouragement; LATE among compliers
designs.tier_qualifier: Tier 1 for the ITT, which inherits exchangeability from randomisation. The LATE additionally requires the exclusion restriction, which is a Tier 2 assumption.
designs.notes: Randomises an offer or nudge rather than the treatment itself, so it suits settings where treatment cannot be withheld

designs.name: Sharp regression discontinuity
designs.estimand: ATE at the cutoff
designs.notes: Requires a continuous running variable and a cutoff that is actually enforced

designs.name: Fuzzy regression discontinuity
designs.estimand: LATE among compliers at the cutoff
designs.notes: Absorbs the former iv_frd entry: fuzzy RD and fuzzy-RD-as-IV are one design under two estimation framings, not two designs

designs.name: Instrumental variables
designs.estimand: LATE among compliers
designs.notes: The exclusion restriction is argued on substantive grounds and cannot be tested

designs.name: Difference-in-differences (2x2)
designs.estimand: ATT
designs.notes: One treatment date. Parallel trends can only be examined where more than one pre-period exists

designs.name: Staggered-adoption difference-in-differences
designs.estimand: Group-time ATT; aggregated to an overall ATT
designs.notes: Kept separate from the 2x2 case because variation in treatment timing is a different data requirement. TWFE can carry negative weights here; the other estimators correct this

designs.name: Synthetic control
designs.estimand: ATT for the treated unit
designs.notes: For one or a few treated units. Needs a donor pool and a long pre-period; the augmented estimator is the fallback where pre-period fit is poor

designs.name: Controlled interrupted time series
designs.estimand: Change in level and slope relative to a control series
designs.notes: The control series is what lifts this above a single series. Placed at Tier 3 by sign-off rather than Tier 2

designs.name: Regression discontinuity in time
designs.estimand: Effect at the date of the policy change
designs.notes: Placed at Tier 3 by sign-off: continuity across a date is a time-series claim that nothing else changed, not local randomisation

designs.name: Matching
designs.estimand: ATT or ATE on the region of common support
designs.tier_qualifier: Upper Tier 4 where prior outcomes are matched on and comparability is demonstrated rather than asserted
designs.notes: Blocks on covariate richness. Balance diagnostics are the characteristic check

designs.name: Weighting
designs.estimand: ATE or ATT
designs.notes: Kept separate from matching because it blocks on positivity rather than covariate richness, and extreme weights are its characteristic failure mode

designs.name: G-computation and standardisation
designs.estimand: ATE or ATT
designs.notes: Models the outcome rather than treatment assignment, so model specification rather than balance is the diagnostic

designs.name: G-methods for time-varying treatment
designs.estimand: Effect of a treatment strategy sustained over time
designs.notes: For confounders that are themselves affected by prior treatment, where conventional adjustment is biased in both directions

designs.name: Interrupted time series
designs.estimand: Change in level and slope at the interruption
designs.notes: No comparison group, so the verdict rests entirely on the pre-intervention trend having continued. Segmented regression is the usual estimator, not a separate design

designs.name: Contribution analysis
designs.estimand: Confidence in a stated contribution claim
designs.notes: Builds a structured causal narrative; requires no counterfactual

designs.name: Realist evaluation
designs.estimand: Context-mechanism-outcome configurations
designs.notes: Requires stakeholder access to elicit mechanisms

designs.name: Process tracing
designs.estimand: Confidence in a hypothesised causal pathway
designs.notes: Requires documentary or interview evidence at each step of the pathway

questions.text: What kind of claim do you need to make?
questions.hint: This decides which part of the tool applies. Only causal claims need a counterfactual design; description and prediction have their own, different standards.

options.label: Describe what is happening, or who is affected
Predict who is likely to experience an outcome
Establish whether an intervention caused a change

questions.text: Is the intervention clearly defined and documented?
questions.hint: What it consists of, who delivers it, and at what intensity. Without this, an observed effect cannot be attributed to the intervention rather than to variation in delivery.

questions.text: Does a theory of change or logic model exist?
questions.hint: A causal model linking the intervention to expected outcomes. Without one it is unclear what the evaluation should measure or how to interpret what it finds.

questions.text: Is the intervention operating at sufficient scale and maturity?
questions.hint: Evaluating impact while delivery is still stabilising risks measuring the immaturity of the intervention rather than its effectiveness.

questions.text: Can the evaluation be planned before the intervention reaches participants?
questions.hint: Randomised designs require allocation to be decided in advance. If the intervention has already rolled out, only observational designs remain available.

options.label: Yes — the evaluation can be designed in advance
No — the intervention has already been delivered or allocated

questions.text: What barriers are there to randomising who receives the intervention?
questions.hint: Ethical, legal, political or operational. Many common objections are addressed by a design adaptation rather than by abandoning randomisation.

options.label: Some, likely addressable by design adaptation

questions.text: What is the natural unit of allocation?
questions.hint: Where the intervention is delivered to whole sites, classes or caseloads, individuals within them cannot be allocated separately.

options.label: Groups — sites, teams, areas or caseloads

questions.text: How many clusters could be allocated?
questions.hint: For a cluster design, precision is governed by the number of clusters far more than by the number of people within them.

questions.text: Is there a phased rollout whose order you could set?
questions.hint: Where everyone is treated eventually but not at once, randomising the order gives a stepped-wedge design without withholding the intervention from anyone.

options.label: Yes — the order is ours to decide
No — the order is fixed or externally determined

questions.text: Would delaying the intervention for part of the group be acceptable?
questions.hint: Everyone receives the intervention; some receive it later, forming a temporary comparison.

questions.text: Does the outcome return to baseline once the intervention stops?
questions.hint: Required for a crossover design, where participants act as their own control.

options.label: Yes — the effect does not persist

questions.text: Can a washout period be built in between conditions?
questions.hint: A gap long enough for the first condition's effect to dissipate before the second begins.

questions.text: Is there a way to encourage take-up without assigning the intervention itself?
questions.hint: An invitation, reminder or incentive offered at random. Useful where the intervention cannot be withheld but take-up is voluntary.

questions.text: Is there genuine uncertainty about whether the intervention works?
questions.hint: Randomisation is hard to justify where the intervention is already known to be effective or known to be harmful.

options.label: Yes — the effect is genuinely uncertain
No — the effect is considered established

questions.text: Is the intervention assigned by a score, date or threshold?
questions.hint: An eligibility cutoff on a continuous measure — a risk score, an age, an income boundary. Those just either side of it are comparable.

questions.text: How strictly is the cutoff followed in practice?
questions.hint: Strict enforcement gives a sharp design. Partial compliance gives a fuzzy design, which estimates an effect only for those whose treatment the cutoff actually changed.

options.label: Mostly — the cutoff shifts the probability of treatment

questions.text: Could people position themselves either side of the cutoff?
questions.hint: If the score can be influenced by those it affects, the comparison breaks down. A density test checks for bunching at the cutoff.

questions.text: How many observations fall close to the cutoff?
questions.hint: Only observations near the cutoff identify the effect. The total sample is not the relevant quantity here.

questions.text: Is there a factor that shifts take-up but has no other route to the outcome?
questions.hint: Distance to a service, a lottery, an administrative quirk. Its credibility rests on an argument about mechanism, not on a statistical test.

questions.text: How strongly does that factor predict take-up?
questions.hint: A weak instrument gives badly behaved estimates. The conventional first-stage F above 10 is a rule of thumb, and a contested one.

questions.text: Can you argue the factor affects the outcome only through take-up?
questions.hint: This cannot be tested. It is defended on substantive grounds, and it is where most instrumental-variable designs fail.

options.label: Yes — a clear substantive argument exists

questions.text: How much outcome data do you have from before the intervention?
questions.hint: Pre-intervention periods are what make a trend testable rather than assumed. One period permits a difference but allows no check on whether the groups were moving together.

questions.text: Is there a group that did not receive the intervention but is otherwise similar?
questions.hint: Another region, service, cohort or eligibility group facing comparable conditions.

questions.text: Did the two groups move together before the intervention?
questions.hint: The central assumption of a difference-based design. It is examined in the pre-period, never proved — the periods after the intervention are exactly what cannot be checked.

questions.text: Did different groups start at different times?
questions.hint: Variation in start dates can strengthen a design, but it also makes the conventional estimator unreliable, so it changes which estimator is appropriate.

options.label: No — a single common start date

questions.text: Are there untreated units that resemble the treated one?
questions.hint: A synthetic control builds a comparison by weighting several untreated units. It needs enough candidates for the weighted combination to track the treated unit beforehand.

questions.text: Is there an equivalent time series for an unaffected group?
questions.hint: A control series distinguishes a change caused by the intervention from one that was happening anyway.

questions.text: Is the date the intervention took effect precisely known?
questions.hint: Required where the comparison is between the periods either side of a change.

questions.text: Did anything else change at the same time?
questions.hint: Other policies, funding changes or external shocks coinciding with the intervention cannot be separated from it in a time-series comparison.

questions.text: How much do you know about the characteristics of both groups?
questions.hint: Adjustment can only account for what is measured. The question is whether you hold the variables that drove who received the intervention.

options.label: Extensive, for treated and untreated alike

questions.text: Do treated and untreated units actually resemble each other?
questions.hint: Where no untreated unit resembles a treated one, no comparison exists for it. This is positivity, and it is checked rather than assumed.

options.label: Limited — overlap only in part of the range

questions.text: Are the main reasons people received the intervention captured in your data?
questions.hint: List the drivers of selection, then check which you actually hold. What is left over is what adjustment cannot fix.

options.label: Some known drivers are not measured

questions.text: Does treatment at one point change the factors that drive later treatment?
questions.hint: Common in ongoing services, where a response to the intervention affects whether it continues. Conventional adjustment is biased here, in either direction.

options.label: Yes — treatment and confounders evolve together

questions.text: Do you hold repeated measures of treatment and of the confounders over time?
questions.hint: Required to model the feedback between treatment and the factors that affect it.

questions.text: How many time points do you have before and after the intervention?
questions.hint: A trend has to be estimated on each side of the interruption. Roughly eight points per segment is a common minimum, and a convention rather than a derived figure.

options.label: Roughly four to eight each side

questions.text: Is there a plan to account for correlation between adjacent time points?
questions.hint: Observations close in time resemble each other. Ignoring this makes the effect look more precisely estimated than it is.

questions.text: Can you speak to the people who deliver and receive the intervention?
questions.hint: Required to elicit how the intervention is meant to work, and for whom.

questions.text: Is there documentation covering each step of the intended causal chain?
questions.hint: Records, monitoring data, case files or correspondence evidencing what happened at each stage.

questions.text: What is your primary intended analytical approach?
questions.hint: This decides which set of questions follows. Sample size serves a different purpose under each: controlling error rates, or achieving precision for a decision.

options.label: Frequentist — significance testing and confidence intervals
Bayesian — posterior distributions and credible intervals
Both — a frequentist primary analysis with Bayesian support, or the reverse

questions.text: What kind of outcome are you measuring?
questions.hint: The outcome type governs which sizing formula applies and what varies.

options.label: Continuous — a score, cost or duration
Count — how many times something happened
Time to event — how long until something happened

questions.text: Are outcomes grouped within sites, practitioners or caseloads?
questions.hint: Outcomes for people sharing a site resemble each other, so they carry less information than the same number of unrelated observations.

questions.text: How much loss to follow-up do you expect?
questions.hint: Attrition reduces the usable sample and, where it differs between groups, threatens the comparison itself rather than only its precision.

questions.text: Is the number of units fixed by context, or can you choose it?
questions.hint: This reverses the question. Where the sample can be chosen, you size it to a target. Where it is fixed, you ask what that sample can and cannot establish.

options.label: It can be chosen — recruitment or rollout is still open
It is fixed — the caseload or cohort is what it is

questions.text: What is the smallest effect that would be worth detecting?
questions.hint: Not the effect you hope for — the smallest one that would still change a decision. Sizing on an optimistic effect is the most common way studies end up underpowered.

questions.text: Who set that figure, and on what basis?
questions.hint: A minimum detectable effect set by the analyst to make the sample work is a circular justification. It should come from the decision or from prior evidence.

options.label: From the decision — the effect that changes what we would do
From prior evidence on similar interventions
From a convention — a standardised effect size benchmark

questions.text: Where do your baseline rate and variability estimates come from?
questions.hint: Every sizing calculation rests on these. An estimate from a different population or period can be badly wrong in either direction.

options.label: From a comparable population or an earlier period
From published literature on other settings

questions.text: Have the significance level and target power been agreed?
questions.hint: Conventionally 5% and 80% or 90%. Both are conventions rather than derived figures, and worth stating rather than inheriting.

questions.text: How many outcomes will be tested, and is there a plan for multiplicity?
questions.hint: Testing many outcomes without a plan inflates the chance of a spurious positive, and is the usual route to a finding that does not replicate.

options.label: One primary outcome, designated in advance
Several outcomes with a stated adjustment or hierarchy

questions.text: Do you have an intracluster correlation estimate?
questions.hint: Required to size a clustered design. The result is sensitive to the value assumed, so a range matters more than a point estimate.

options.label: From published estimates in this field

questions.text: Has expected attrition been built into the sizing?
questions.hint: Sizing on the recruited sample rather than the analysed sample overstates precision.

options.label: Yes — with scenarios for different rates
Yes, at a single assumed rate

questions.text: Will there be interim analyses?
questions.hint: Looking at the data repeatedly and stopping when significant inflates the error rate unless the analysis plan accounts for it.

options.label: No — a single analysis at the end
Yes, with a pre-specified spending function

questions.text: Will the sizing be reported across a range of assumptions?
questions.hint: Variance, baseline rate and intracluster correlation are all estimates. A single number implies more certainty about the design than exists.

options.label: Yes — a range for each key input

questions.text: Will the analysis be pre-registered or otherwise recorded before data are seen?
questions.hint: The protection against analytic choices being made, knowingly or not, to favour a result.

options.label: Yes — registered or lodged in advance

questions.text: What size of effect would change the decision?
questions.hint: The analysis can then report the probability that the effect exceeds it — which is the question a decision-maker actually asked, and one a significance test cannot answer.

options.label: Agreed with those making the decision

questions.text: Is there a range of effects you would treat as equivalent to no effect?
questions.hint: A region of practical equivalence lets the analysis conclude that an effect is negligible, rather than only failing to find one. Its bounds are a judgement about what the decision treats as too small to matter, not a statistical quantity.

options.label: Yes — bounds set by those making the decision

questions.text: Where does your prior come from?
questions.hint: The most consequential question at small sample sizes, because the prior supplies what the data cannot.

options.label: From previous evaluations of similar interventions
A weakly informative default, chosen to contribute little

questions.text: By what protocol were the expert judgements elicited?
questions.hint: A named protocol makes the prior auditable. SHELF trains experts first, takes individual judgements before discussion to limit anchoring, then fits a consensus distribution.

options.label: Cooke's Classical Method, with calibration questions

questions.text: How much of the posterior will come from the prior rather than the data?
questions.hint: At small sample sizes this can be most of it. That is not disqualifying, but it has to be known and reported — otherwise the finding restates the assumption.

options.label: Expected to be small, not yet checked

questions.text: Is a prior sensitivity analysis planned?
questions.hint: Re-running under alternative priors, including a sceptical one. The standard reviewer challenge, and a stated regulatory expectation.

options.label: Yes — with alternatives specified in advance

questions.text: What will you do if the prior and the data disagree?
questions.hint: Foreseeable, and better decided before the data arrive than after. Discovering the conflict and then choosing a response is how a prior becomes unfalsifiable.

options.label: A stated plan, agreed in advance

questions.text: What target will size the study, or characterise it if the sample is fixed?
questions.hint: Where the sample can be chosen: a target assurance, or a target credible interval width. Where it is fixed: the precision the sample can be expected to deliver.

options.label: Assurance — the probability the study gives a usable answer
Precision — a target credible interval width
Expected utility or value of information

questions.text: Will the audience expect frequentist error-rate guarantees?
questions.hint: Common where findings go to a board or an external reviewer accustomed to p-values. Operating characteristics can be simulated, but that has to be planned.

options.label: No — a probabilistic answer will be accepted
Yes, and operating characteristics will be simulated

questions.text: Will the design adapt or stop early based on accumulating data?
questions.hint: Adaptive stopping is a genuine advantage of the Bayesian approach, and its behaviour has to be simulated rather than assumed.

options.label: No — a single analysis at the end

blockers.message: Allocation cannot be randomised once the intervention has already been delivered.
Randomisation has been ruled out, so no randomised design is available.
The intervention is delivered to whole groups, so individuals within them cannot be allocated separately.

conditions.message: Significant barriers to randomisation were identified.
conditions.unlock: Check whether a stepped-wedge, waitlist or encouragement design addresses the specific objection — these are often accepted where straightforward randomisation is not.

conditions.message: The effect is considered already established, which makes withholding the intervention hard to justify.
conditions.unlock: Document the remaining uncertainty, or move to a design that withholds nothing.

conditions.message: Stakeholders disagree about whether the effect is already established.
conditions.unlock: Resolve this before an ethics application, since it is the usual ground for refusal.

blockers.message: Allocation cannot be randomised once the intervention has already been delivered.
Randomisation has been ruled out, so no randomised design is available.
The intervention is delivered to individuals, so there are no natural clusters to allocate.

conditions.message: Fewer than about 15 clusters. Precision in a cluster design is governed by the number of clusters, so a large number of individuals within them does not compensate.
conditions.unlock: Establish whether more clusters can be recruited, or whether individual allocation is possible after all.

conditions.message: Significant barriers to randomisation were identified.
conditions.unlock: Check whether randomising the order of a phased rollout is acceptable instead.

warnings.message: A cluster design needs an intracluster correlation estimate to size properly. With this few clusters the result is sensitive to the value assumed, so take a range to your statistician rather than a single figure.

blockers.message: The rollout order cannot be randomised once delivery has happened.
The rollout order is fixed or externally determined, so there is nothing left to randomise.

conditions.message: Only partial influence over the sequencing of the rollout.
conditions.unlock: Establish which part of the order is genuinely open. Randomising even a subset of the sequence can be enough.

conditions.message: Too few clusters to allocate across a useful number of steps.
conditions.unlock: Establish whether more sites can join, or whether fewer, larger steps would work.

warnings.message: In a stepped-wedge design every unit is treated later in the study than it is untreated, so the treatment effect is entangled with any underlying time trend. The analysis must adjust for time.

blockers.message: Allocation cannot be randomised once the intervention has already been delivered.
The outcome does not return to baseline, so a participant cannot serve as their own control in a later period.
Without a washout period the first condition contaminates the second.

conditions.message: Whether the effect persists has not been established.
conditions.unlock: Check the evidence on how long the effect lasts; this determines both whether a crossover is possible and how long the washout must be.

conditions.message: The feasibility of a washout period has not been established.
conditions.unlock: Establish the minimum gap needed, then whether delivery can accommodate it.

blockers.message: Allocation cannot be randomised once the intervention has already been delivered.
A waitlist design requires part of the group to receive the intervention later.

conditions.message: Whether a delay is acceptable has not been settled.
conditions.unlock: Agree the maximum tolerable wait with delivery colleagues. That wait is also the window in which the effect must be measured.

warnings.message: The comparison exists only until the waitlist group is treated, so the design measures a short-run effect. Outcomes that take longer to emerge cannot be captured this way.

blockers.message: The encouragement cannot be randomised once the intervention has been delivered.
No credible way to encourage take-up without assigning the intervention itself, which is what this design requires.

conditions.message: A possible encouragement has been identified but not established.
conditions.unlock: Check that it moves take-up appreciably. A weak encouragement yields an estimate for too few people to be useful.

conditions.message: The encouragement must affect the outcome only by changing take-up. If it carries information or incentive that acts directly, the complier estimate is biased.
conditions.unlock: Set out why the encouragement has no direct route to the outcome. This cannot be tested, so it has to be argued.

warnings.message: This estimates the effect for those whose take-up the encouragement changed, not for everyone. Those people may differ from the population the decision is about.

blockers.message: A discontinuity design requires assignment by a score, date or threshold.
The cutoff shifts the probability of treatment rather than determining it, which is a fuzzy design rather than a sharp one.
Sorting around the cutoff means those either side differ in ways beyond treatment, which removes the basis for the comparison.

conditions.message: Whether people can position themselves around the cutoff has not been tested.
conditions.unlock: Run a density test for bunching at the cutoff, and check whether those it affects could know the rule and act on it.

conditions.message: How strictly the cutoff is applied in practice has not been established.
conditions.unlock: Examine administrative records to see how often the rule was overridden. This decides between a sharp and a fuzzy design.

conditions.message: Few observations fall near the cutoff, and only those identify the effect. A large total sample does not help.
conditions.unlock: Count observations within a plausible bandwidth rather than in the dataset as a whole, and take that figure to a power calculation.

warnings.message: The estimate depends on the bandwidth chosen around the cutoff. Report results across a range of bandwidths rather than only the one that was selected.
The result applies at the cutoff. It says little about people far from it, who may be the group the decision concerns.

blockers.message: A discontinuity design requires assignment by a score, date or threshold.
Sorting around the cutoff removes the basis for the comparison.

conditions.message: Whether people can position themselves around the cutoff has not been tested.
conditions.unlock: Run a density test for bunching at the cutoff.

conditions.message: A fuzzy design relies on a clear jump in the probability of treatment at the cutoff. A small jump identifies the effect for very few people.
conditions.unlock: Estimate the size of the jump in take-up at the cutoff before committing.

conditions.message: Few observations near the cutoff, and a fuzzy design needs more than a sharp one.
conditions.unlock: Count observations within a plausible bandwidth and power on that figure.

warnings.message: This estimates the effect for those at the cutoff whose treatment the rule actually changed — a narrower group than a sharp design addresses.

blockers.message: No factor identified that shifts take-up without affecting the outcome by any other route.
Plausible alternative routes from the instrument to the outcome were identified. The exclusion restriction is the whole basis of the design, so this blocks it rather than qualifying it.

conditions.message: A candidate instrument has been identified but not established.
conditions.unlock: Check that it predicts take-up, and set out why it cannot affect the outcome directly.

conditions.message: The exclusion restriction has not yet been considered.
conditions.unlock: Write down every route by which the instrument could reach the outcome, and argue each one away. This cannot be tested statistically.

conditions.message: A weak instrument gives estimates that are biased towards the unadjusted association and confidence intervals that understate uncertainty.
conditions.unlock: Report first-stage strength. The conventional F above 10 is a rule of thumb that recent work shows is not sufficient for valid inference, so treat it as a floor rather than a target.

conditions.message: The strength of the instrument has not been established.
conditions.unlock: Estimate the first stage before committing to the design.

blockers.message: A difference-in-differences comparison requires outcome data from before the intervention.
No comparison group that did not receive the intervention.
The groups were already moving apart before the intervention, so the difference afterwards cannot be attributed to it.
Adoption is or will be staggered, so this is not a two-period comparison. The staggered-adoption design applies instead.

conditions.message: With one pre-period the parallel-trends assumption cannot be examined at all. It would be assumed rather than supported.
conditions.unlock: Find at least two further pre-periods so the trends can be compared.

conditions.message: Whether the groups moved together before the intervention has not been examined.
conditions.unlock: Plot both series across every available pre-period. This is the main thing a reviewer will look for.

conditions.message: A possible comparison group has been identified but its comparability is not established.
conditions.unlock: Check that it faced comparable conditions and was not affected by the intervention itself.

blockers.message: A difference-in-differences comparison requires outcome data from before the intervention.
No comparison group that did not receive the intervention.
All units started at the same time, so there is no variation in timing. The two-period design applies instead.
The groups were already moving apart before the intervention.

conditions.message: Whether the groups moved together before the intervention has not been examined.
conditions.unlock: Compare trends for each adoption cohort separately, not just in aggregate — a single cohort can mask divergence in another.

conditions.message: The staggered rollout is planned but has not begun.
conditions.unlock: If the order is still open, randomising it gives a stepped-wedge design at Tier 1 for no additional data cost.

warnings.message: Under staggered adoption the conventional two-way fixed effects estimator averages comparisons that include already-treated units acting as controls, and can place negative weights on some of them. Use an estimator built for staggered timing — Callaway-Sant'Anna, Sun-Abraham or Borusyak-Jaravel-Spiess. This is an estimator choice; it does not change the tier.

blockers.message: A synthetic control is built by matching the treated unit's pre-intervention path, which requires a run of periods rather than one.
No untreated units available to weight into a comparison.

conditions.message: A short pre-period gives the weighting little to match on, so good pre-period fit may be achieved by chance rather than by genuine similarity.
conditions.unlock: Extend the pre-period if the data allow. Where it cannot be extended, the augmented estimator corrects some of the resulting bias.

conditions.message: Few candidate donor units, of uncertain comparability.
conditions.unlock: Check that donors were not themselves affected by the intervention, and that none experienced its own shock during the period.

warnings.message: Conventional confidence intervals do not apply. Inference is by placebo tests across the donor pool, which is why pool size affects what can be concluded as well as how well the method fits.

blockers.message: No equivalent series for an unaffected group. Without one this is a single interrupted time series at Tier 5.
A pre-intervention trend must be estimable on both series.
The interruption point must be known to separate before from after.

conditions.message: A possible control series has been identified but not established.
conditions.unlock: Check it was genuinely unaffected by the intervention and is subject to the same external influences.

conditions.message: Too few time points to estimate a trend on each side of the interruption with any confidence.
conditions.unlock: Aim for roughly eight points per segment. This is a working convention rather than a derived minimum.

conditions.message: Other changes coincided with the intervention. A control series helps only where it was exposed to those same changes.
conditions.unlock: Establish whether the control series was affected by the same coinciding changes.

conditions.message: Whether anything else changed at the same time has not been checked.
conditions.unlock: Compile a timeline of other policy and funding changes across the study period.

blockers.message: This design compares either side of a date, so the date must be known precisely.
No data from before the change.
Other changes occurred at the same date. With no comparison group there is nothing to separate their effect from the intervention's.

This design estimates locally either side of the date, so it needs observations close to it. With very few time points there is nothing to fit a local comparison to, and a plain interrupted time series over the whole series is the available design instead.

conditions.message: Local estimation around the date rests on the observations nearest it, which are fewer than the length of the series suggests.
conditions.unlock: Count the observations within a plausible window either side of the date rather than across the whole series, and power on that figure.

conditions.message: The date is approximate or the change was phased, which blurs the discontinuity.
conditions.unlock: Establish a precise date. Where the change was genuinely phased, a design built on the phasing is likely to serve better.

conditions.message: Whether anything else changed at the same date has not been checked.
conditions.unlock: Compile a timeline around the date. This is the main threat to the design, so it needs doing before committing to it.

warnings.message: Placed at Tier 3 rather than Tier 2: continuity across a date is a claim that nothing else changed then, which is a time-series argument rather than local randomisation. Some sources place it higher where the cutoff is externally imposed.

blockers.message: Matching can only adjust for what is measured. With little covariate data there is nothing to match on.
Where treated and untreated units barely resemble each other there are no comparable pairs to form.

conditions.message: Overlap exists only across part of the range, so any estimate applies to that part and not to the whole population.
conditions.unlock: Define the region of common support and state that the result applies there. Weighting handles limited overlap better than matching does.

conditions.message: Whether the groups overlap has not been examined.
conditions.unlock: Compare covariate distributions between treated and untreated units before committing.

conditions.message: Known drivers of selection are not in the data. Matching cannot adjust for them and balance diagnostics will not reveal them.
conditions.unlock: Plan a sensitivity analysis quantifying how strong an unmeasured confounder would need to be to overturn the finding.

conditions.message: The drivers of who received the intervention have not been established.
conditions.unlock: List them first, then check which are measured. The gap between the two lists is the design's main weakness.

conditions.message: Covariate data has known gaps.
conditions.unlock: Document which variables are missing and why, so reviewers can judge the residual risk.

warnings.message: Good balance on measured covariates is not evidence that unmeasured confounding is absent. It shows the matching worked, not that the assumption holds.

Pre-intervention outcome data is available. Matching on prior outcomes as well as characteristics places this at the upper end of Tier 4, and the Maryland scale allows level 3 where comparability is demonstrated rather than asserted.

blockers.message: Weighting can only adjust for what is measured.
Where some units had almost no chance of receiving the intervention, their weights become extreme and the estimate is driven by a handful of observations. This is a positivity violation.

conditions.message: Limited overlap produces large weights that dominate the estimate.
conditions.unlock: Use overlap weights or trimming, which target the population where the comparison is actually supported, and report how many observations the weights concentrate on.

conditions.message: Whether the groups overlap has not been examined.
conditions.unlock: Examine the distribution of estimated propensity scores in both groups before committing; this is what determines whether weighting is viable at all.

conditions.message: Known drivers of selection are not in the data.
conditions.unlock: Plan a sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding.

conditions.message: The drivers of who received the intervention have not been established.
conditions.unlock: List them, then check which are measured.

warnings.message: Report the distribution of the weights alongside the estimate. A result resting on a few heavily weighted observations is fragile even where the average looks sound.

blockers.message: Standardisation models the outcome given the covariates, so it needs those covariates to be measured.
With no overlap the outcome model would extrapolate into regions where no comparable units exist, which the method cannot signal.

conditions.message: Known drivers of selection are not in the data.
conditions.unlock: Plan a sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding.

conditions.message: The drivers of who received the intervention have not been established.
conditions.unlock: List them, then check which are measured.

conditions.message: Overlap has not been examined, and extrapolation beyond it is silent here.
conditions.unlock: Check overlap even though this method does not require it as directly as matching, because the model will extrapolate without warning.

warnings.message: The estimate depends on the outcome model being correctly specified. A doubly-robust estimator gives a second chance: it remains consistent if either the outcome model or the treatment model is right.

blockers.message: Treatment is a one-off, so conventional adjustment is appropriate and simpler. The g-methods exist for feedback between treatment and confounders.
Modelling the feedback between treatment and confounders requires repeated measures of both.
The time-varying confounders must themselves be measured.

conditions.message: Whether treatment affects later confounders has not been established.
conditions.unlock: Draw the causal structure over time. If no arrow runs from treatment to a later confounder, a simpler design will serve.

conditions.message: Known drivers of selection are not in the data. The g-methods address confounding by measured time-varying factors; they do nothing about unmeasured ones.
conditions.unlock: Plan a sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding.

warnings.message: Where treatment affects later confounders, adjusting for them conventionally blocks part of the effect, while omitting them leaves confounding. Both directions are wrong, which is why a g-method is needed rather than preferred.

blockers.message: The whole design rests on estimating the pre-intervention trend, so pre-period data is required.
The interruption point must be known.
Other changes coincided with the intervention. With no comparison group there is nothing to distinguish their effect from the intervention's.

conditions.message: Too few time points to estimate a trend on each side of the interruption.
conditions.unlock: Aim for roughly eight points per segment. A working convention rather than a derived minimum, so treat it as a range.

conditions.message: Enough points to fit a model, but not enough to characterise the trend confidently.
conditions.unlock: Extend the series if the data allow, and report the estimate's sensitivity to the window chosen.

conditions.message: Adjacent time points resemble each other. Ignoring this makes the effect appear more precisely estimated than it is.
conditions.unlock: Test for autocorrelation and model it, or use an estimator that accounts for it.

conditions.message: Whether anything else changed at the same time has not been checked.
conditions.unlock: Compile a timeline of other changes across the study period. Without a comparison group this is the design's central vulnerability.

warnings.message: Nothing here can test whether the pre-intervention trend would have continued. If a control series can be found the design moves to Tier 3 for no extra data on the treated unit.

conditions.message: Contribution analysis tests a stated theory of change. Without one there is no claim to assess.
conditions.unlock: Develop a theory of change with delivery staff and stakeholders. That work is part of the evaluation rather than a prerequisite for it.

conditions.message: The theory of change is still in development.
conditions.unlock: Finalise the causal chain and the assumptions at each link before gathering evidence against it.

conditions.message: Evidence for the steps in the causal chain is patchy.
conditions.unlock: Identify which links are least evidenced; those determine what can be concluded.

warnings.message: The output is confidence in a contribution claim, not an effect size. Where a number is needed for a business case, this will not produce one.

blockers.message: Realist evaluation works by eliciting mechanisms from those who deliver and receive the intervention. Without access to them the method has no input.

conditions.message: Limited access to the people involved in delivery.
conditions.unlock: Establish which groups can be reached. Partial access narrows which context-mechanism-outcome configurations can be examined rather than ruling the method out.

warnings.message: Findings are explicitly about what works for whom in which context. They do not generalise in the way an average effect is assumed to.

blockers.message: Process tracing tests a causal pathway step by step against evidence. Without documentation of those steps there is nothing to trace.

conditions.message: Documentation covers only part of the hypothesised pathway.
conditions.unlock: Identify which steps lack evidence. A pathway can still be assessed where the gaps are at links that carry less of the argument.

conditions.message: There is no stated pathway to trace.
conditions.unlock: Set out the hypothesised causal chain before gathering evidence against it.

warnings.message: Conclusions apply within the case examined. Establishing that a mechanism operated here is not evidence about how often it operates elsewhere.

stages.label: Explore
stages.gloss: Understanding the problem and who it affects, before an intervention has been designed.

stages.label: Co-design
stages.gloss: Developing the intervention with the people who will deliver and receive it, and setting out how it is meant to work.

stages.label: Test
stages.gloss: Trying specific components or mechanisms to find out what works, while the intervention is still being refined.

stages.label: Grow
stages.gloss: Evaluating a stable, fully specified intervention operating at scale.

readiness.question: intervention_defined
readiness.message: The intervention is not yet specified, so an observed change could not be attributed to it rather than to variation in what was delivered. No impact evaluation design resolves this.
readiness.redirect: Document what the intervention consists of, who delivers it and at what intensity. A process evaluation can describe and standardise delivery first.

readiness.question: theory_of_change
readiness.message: With no theory of change there is nothing to say which outcomes should move, over what period, or how a result should be read. The evaluation would have no stated expectation to test.
readiness.redirect: Develop a logic model with delivery staff and stakeholders. A developmental evaluation can support this while the intervention is still forming.

readiness.question: maturity
readiness.message: The intervention is early or small-scale, so an evaluation now would largely measure its immaturity rather than its effect.
readiness.redirect: Consider a process or developmental evaluation while delivery stabilises. Where a specific component is already settled, a Test-stage evaluation of that component may still be worthwhile.

inference.note: The work needed is specifying the intervention, which is Co-design activity.
Articulating how the intervention is meant to work is Co-design activity.
Where the intervention is early and small, the useful work is understanding the problem and the delivery context rather than estimating an effect.

Something is still settling, so the appropriate estimand is the effect of a specific component or mechanism rather than of the whole programme. Every impact evaluation design remains available; what narrows is the claim being made.

Defined, theorised and at scale. Both stages apply: the distinction is whether the programme model is still being refined (Test) or is stable and being evaluated at full scale (Grow). Identification requirements are identical, so no design is excluded by the choice between them.

routing.note: Prediction questions are answered by modelling who is likely to experience an outcome. They do not need a counterfactual and do not belong on the ladder.
Descriptive and contextual questions are served by the qualitative strand. Sending them to a counterfactual design would answer a question that was not asked.
Causal claims need a counterfactual design. The Design Finder runs the same engine over a minimal question set as a quick screen.
Continuing to the full assessment keeps every answer already given and asks only what the remaining rungs require.
Where the tree establishes that the question is causal after all, the ladder applies.
Where a readiness gate fires, the useful next step is the theory-based and qualitative strand — process, developmental or contribution work — not a counterfactual design.

nhst.label: Frequentist (null hypothesis significance testing)
nhst.sample_role: The sample controls error rates. It buys power to detect an effect of a chosen size at a chosen significance level, and the calculation runs from an effect you have to nominate in advance.

tensions.message: The smallest effect worth detecting has not been established, or has no stated basis. Where it is chosen to make an available sample look adequate, the calculation justifies itself.
tensions.prompt: Ask what effect would actually change the decision, and whether the study can detect one that small. If it cannot, that is worth knowing before fieldwork rather than after.

tensions.message: The baseline rate and variability are assumed rather than sourced. Every figure in the sizing calculation rests on them.
tensions.prompt: Ask what happens to the required sample if the baseline is a third higher or lower than assumed. If the answer changes the design, the estimate needs a source.

tensions.message: Several outcomes will be tested with no stated adjustment or hierarchy. The chance of at least one spurious positive rises with each one.
tensions.prompt: Ask which single outcome the decision rests on, and whether the others are secondary or exploratory. Record that before the data arrive.

tensions.message: The design is clustered but the intracluster correlation is assumed or absent. The required number of clusters is sensitive to this value.
tensions.prompt: Ask for the required sample across a range of plausible correlations rather than at one value, and whether the design still works at the pessimistic end.

tensions.message: Interim analyses are planned with no stated adjustment. Repeatedly testing and stopping on significance inflates the error rate the design is meant to control.
tensions.prompt: Ask for a spending function or a formal stopping rule, agreed before the first look at the data.

tensions.message: The sizing rests on a single value for each input. Variance, baseline and correlation are all estimates, so one number implies more certainty about the design than exists.
tensions.prompt: Ask for the sample size across a range for each key input, and which input the answer is most sensitive to.

bayesian.label: Bayesian
bayesian.sample_role: The sample buys precision for a decision. A small sample does not invalidate the inference — the posterior is as coherent at twenty units as at twenty thousand — but it does mean the prior supplies more of the answer. That is acceptable where the prior can be defended, and not otherwise.

tensions.message: The prior has no stated source, or rests on informal discussion rather than a documented elicitation. At small sample sizes the prior supplies much of the posterior, so an unexaminable prior makes the finding unexaminable.
tensions.prompt: Ask whether previous evaluations could supply the prior instead, and if expert judgement is the only option, whether a structured elicitation such as SHELF is practicable — individual judgements taken before group discussion, with the basis recorded.

tensions.message: Neither a decision threshold nor a region of practical equivalence has been agreed. Without one the posterior cannot be turned into a decision, and the analysis reduces to reporting an interval.
tensions.prompt: Ask those making the decision what size of effect would change it, and what size they would treat as too small to matter. Those two answers are what the analysis reports against.

tensions.message: An informative prior is in use but its contribution to the posterior has not been quantified. Where the prior supplies most of the answer, the finding largely restates what was assumed — and a Bayesian analysis chosen to rescue an underpowered study will do exactly that without saying so.
tensions.prompt: Ask for the prior's effective sample size alongside the actual one, and for the posterior under a deliberately sceptical prior. If the conclusion changes, the study is reporting its assumptions.

tensions.message: No prior sensitivity analysis is planned. This is the standard reviewer challenge and a stated regulatory expectation.
tensions.prompt: Ask which alternative priors will be run — at minimum a sceptical one and a weakly informative one — and agree them before the data are seen.

tensions.message: The audience expects frequentist error-rate guarantees but no simulation is planned to provide them. A posterior probability does not answer a question about long-run error rates.
tensions.prompt: Ask whether the operating characteristics can be simulated — the false positive and false negative rates the design would show across repeated hypothetical studies — or whether the audience can be brought to a probabilistic answer.

tensions.message: The design stops early on accumulating data without simulated operating characteristics. Adaptive stopping is a real advantage of the approach, and its behaviour has to be established rather than assumed.
tensions.prompt: Ask for simulations across a range of true effects, including no effect, showing how often the rule stops early and what it concludes when it does.

undecided_comparison.nhst: Controls error rates — power to detect an effect of a nominated size at a chosen significance level.
undecided_comparison.bayesian: Buys precision or assurance for a decision. The prior and the data share the work, and their shares can be reported.

undecided_comparison.nhst: The smallest effect worth detecting, and who set it.
undecided_comparison.bayesian: The effect that would change the decision, and the range treated as equivalent to no effect.

undecided_comparison.nhst: A baseline rate and variability from a credible source; a significance level and target power; a multiplicity plan if several outcomes are tested.
undecided_comparison.bayesian: Where the prior comes from and who accepts it; a target interval width or assurance; a plan for prior-data conflict.

undecided_comparison.topic: If the sample is already fixed
undecided_comparison.nhst: Ask what the minimum detectable effect is, and whether it is plausible.
undecided_comparison.bayesian: Ask what posterior precision to expect, and how much of it comes from the prior rather than the data.

undecided_comparison.nhst: Number of clusters and the intracluster correlation; attrition scenarios.
undecided_comparison.bayesian: The same, plus priors on variation between clusters, which are themselves estimates needing a source.

undecided_comparison.nhst: A pre-specified analysis, with a spending function if interim looks are planned.
undecided_comparison.bayesian: Posterior-probability stopping rules, with simulated operating characteristics.

undecided_comparison.nhst: Ranges for variance and intracluster correlation.
undecided_comparison.bayesian: Alternative priors, including a sceptical one, and a plan for prior-data conflict.
Whether readers expect frequentist error-rate calibration, and whether operating characteristics will be simulated if so.

design_quantities.note: Clusters before cluster size. Adding people to existing sites buys far less than adding sites, and beyond a point buys almost nothing.

design_quantities.quantity: Clusters and the number of steps
design_quantities.note: The sequence length matters as well as the number of units in it.

design_quantities.quantity: People randomised, and the length of the window before crossover
design_quantities.note: The comparison exists only until the waitlist group is treated.

design_quantities.quantity: Those whose take-up the encouragement changed
design_quantities.note: Not those randomised. A weak encouragement gives a large study that identifies the effect for very few people.

design_quantities.quantity: Observations within a plausible bandwidth of the cutoff
design_quantities.note: Not the total sample. A large dataset can be thin where it matters.

design_quantities.quantity: Observations near the cutoff, and the size of the jump in take-up
design_quantities.note: A fuzzy design needs more than a sharp one at the same cutoff.

design_quantities.quantity: Sample size and first-stage strength together
design_quantities.note: A large sample does not compensate for a weak instrument.

design_quantities.quantity: Treated and comparison units, and pre-intervention periods
Treated and comparison units, adoption cohorts, and pre-periods
design_quantities.note: Each adoption cohort is its own comparison, so cohort size matters as well as total.

design_quantities.quantity: Donor pool size and pre-period length
design_quantities.note: Inference is by placebo tests across the donor pool, so pool size governs what can be concluded as well as how well the method fits.

design_quantities.quantity: Time points per segment, on both series
Observations within a window either side of the date
Units in the region of common support
design_quantities.note: Not the full sample — unmatched units contribute nothing.
Can be far below the nominal count where a few observations carry large weights. Worth computing before committing.

design_quantities.quantity: Units with complete treatment and confounder histories
design_quantities.note: Incomplete histories drop out of the analysis rather than being partially used.

design_quantities.quantity: Number of time points, and the degree of autocorrelation
design_quantities.note: Correlated observations carry less information than their count suggests, so the effective number is lower than the nominal one.

ready_reckoner.note: Illustrative only. Produces a rough figure from the user's own inputs to support a conversation with a statistician — not a substitute for one, and never an input to any verdict the tool reaches.

modes.outputs: A rough minimum detectable effect for the stated sample, outcome type, baseline and intracluster correlation.
A rough expected credible interval width, and the share of the posterior precision contributed by the prior rather than the data.
